summary: This informational memo registers MIME sub-types for the Flexible Image Transport System (FITS), a format used by the astronomy community to exchange data such as images. The encoding itself comes from the published FITS standards.

plainLanguage.summary: Astronomers store telescope pictures in a special file type. This document gives that file type an official label so email and the web can recognise it.

subtitle: Registering standard media types for astronomical data files

tldr.problem: Astronomers have used FITS files to exchange telescope data since 1979, but without official MIME type registrations, email and web servers could not properly recognize or handle these files.
tldr.mechanism: This RFC registers two standard MIME types with IANA: application/fits for any FITS data, and image/fits specifically for FITS image arrays, allowing the format to be correctly identified on the internet.
tldr.outcome: FITS files are now properly recognized by email systems and web browsers, supporting the international astronomical community's data exchange infrastructure.

today: RFC 4047 is an Informational RFC and has not been obsoleted or updated. The two MIME types it registers, application/fits and image/fits, remain the standard way to identify FITS files on the internet.

sections.title: Introduction and Background
sections.content:
FITS (Flexible Image Transport System) is a data format designed in the late 1970s to let observatories exchange astronomical data. The format was born out of necessity: scientists needed a way to reliably transfer arrays of numbers (telescope images, spectral data, tables of measurements) between computers with different architectures and operating systems.

Before the World Wide Web, astronomers used FITS over direct file transfer connections. Once HTTP and email became common, the community had to invent their own informal labels for FITS files, but these labels were not recognized by internet infrastructure. This document formally registers two MIME types (media types) with IANA so that email servers, web browsers and other software can automatically identify and handle FITS files correctly.
sections.plainLanguage: Scientists created FITS in the 1970s as a universal way to store and share telescope data. As the internet grew, they needed official labels for these files so computers would understand what they are.

sections.title: The FITS Format
sections.content:
FITS files are built from 2880-byte blocks, a size chosen because it divides evenly across different computer architectures. Each file consists of one or more header and data units (HDUs). The first HDU is the primary HDU (PHDU), and any following HDUs are extension HDUs (XHDUs). Each header is a sequence of 80-character ASCII keyword/value pairs describing the data that follows.

The format supports many data types: N-dimensional image arrays, ASCII tables, and binary tables. A FITS file can hold a single image, multiple images, a catalog as a table, or any combination of these. Keywords in the header convey metadata such as observation dates, instrument settings, and celestial coordinates. The standard has evolved since 1981, adding support for multiple images, tables, and world coordinate systems, while maintaining backward compatibility: files written in 1979 can still be read by modern software.
sections.plainLanguage: FITS files are organized in chunks of 2880 bytes, each holding a header (a list of labels and values) and data (like an image made of numbers). A file can contain one image, many images, or tables of data, and scientists can add extra labels to explain what everything means.

sections.title: The Two MIME Types
sections.content:
application/fits is the general-purpose MIME type for any FITS file. It applies to files with any combination of HDUs: a primary header with table data, multiple images in extension HDUs, or any other configuration allowed by the FITS standard. The PHDU may have zero dimensions (NAXIS=0), acting as a container for extension data. Applications should be able to display a list of all HDUs and their keyword/value pairs.

image/fits is registered for FITS files where the primary HDU contains a single image array. The file SHOULD have a PHDU with a positive NAXIS value (typically 2 for 2D images, but 1D spectra and 3D data cubes are allowed). Image viewers can expect to render the primary array, and may ignore extension HDUs. Multi-dimensional image files should use image/fits, while files where the PHDU is a container (like a catalog table in an extension) should use application/fits.
sections.plainLanguage: The RFC registers two labels: one for any kind of FITS file (application/fits), and one for files that are mainly pictures (image/fits). This helps computers know which program to use when you open the file.

sections.title: Portability and Stability
sections.content:
FITS has a remarkable track record of compatibility. The format was designed with care so that old files remain readable forever. Files written by a FITS program on one type of computer in 1979 can be read by a completely different computer today. The FITS community adopted the principle "Once FITS, always FITS": no change to the standard is allowed if it would invalidate existing files.

The International Astronomical Union established the FITS Working Group in 1988 to oversee the standard. Changes only happen after approval by regional working groups and the IAU. This conservative approach has meant that massive archives holding petabytes of FITS data are safe: the standard will not change in a way that breaks them. The format has supported observations across the entire electromagnetic spectrum, from radio to gamma rays, and is used by ground-based observatories and space missions alike.
sections.plainLanguage: FITS was designed to last. Astronomers promised never to break old files, so a picture from the 1970s can still be read today. Organizations all over the world took control of the standard to make sure it stays stable and useful.
